sections.heading: Abstract:
sections.text:
Developing an effective catalyst to reduce carbon dioxide (CO2) to value-added C2+
products is a key challenge for CO2 utilization. Here we report a core-shell copper with native oxide (Cu@Cu2O) catalyst featuring a thin native oxide layer on the surface grown under ambient conditions. The Cu(I) oxide species on Cu@Cu2O surface remained relatively stable against reduction under CO2 electroreduction condition, and the synergism between surface Cu+ and Cu0 in Cu@Cu2O contributed to boosting its efficiency and selectivity toward C2 products. This Cu@Cu2O catalyst achieved an excellent selectivity (~ 50% at −1.0 V vs reversible hydrogen electrode) for C2 (ethylene and ethanol) production.
Keywords: CO2 reduction; electrocatalyst; copper; native oxide; faradaic efficiency

sections.heading: 1. Introduction
sections.text:
The electrochemical CO2 reduction reaction (CO2RR) under ambient temperature and
pressure suggests a great promise for converting the greenhouse CO2 gas into a variety of potential value-added chemicals [1]. Nonetheless, due to the intrinsic inertness of CO2 and the slow kinetics of the multiple proton-coupled electron transfer (PCET) process, the
realization of such electrocatalysts has remained significantly challenging [2-4]. Among a
large variety of electrocatalysts being investigated, copper- (Cu-) based materials have been
the only known category of candidates that can lead to reduction products with multi-electron (> 2e-) transfer, while typically requiring high overpotentials and yielding poor selectivity [5-
8].
Since the first report of the Cu-based electrocatalyst for CO2 reduction by Hori et al.[9],
significant research efforts have been invested to improve the efficiency and selectivity of
Cu-based catalysts for CO2RR, including but not limited to, composition and morphology tuning [10-14], forming crystal boundaries [15,16] and bimetallic alloys [17-19], and
optimizing the cation [20,21] and pH of the electrolytes [22,23]. For instance, a recent report
of bromide/bromine- induced nanodendritic copper catalysts achieved a maximum ethylene
(C2H4) faradic efficiency of 57% [24], which was ascribed to the high- index facets containing low-coordinated sites. Besides, an oxide-derived approach was also developed for a class of Cu-based CO2RR catalysts with improved activity and high selectivity at low overpotentials [15,16,25-30]. It was proposed that the grain boundaries on the oxide-derived Cu surface
serve as strong binding sites for *CO intermediates, thereby enhancing the subsequent
reduction of *CO to hydrocarbons. Beyond that, recent reports confirmed that Cu(I) species
in copper-based catalysts can remain relatively stable during CO2RR and play a critical role in promoting the efficiency and selectivity of CO2RR, but their functions are still ambiguous [27,31-34]. Very recently, theoretical calculations showed that the synergetic effect between
Cu(I) and surface Cu(0) in copper-based catalyst promotes both the CO2 activation and *CO dimerization processes, and thereby improves thermodynamics and kinetics for C2 production [35]. Nonetheless, to date, almost all the reports on the oxide-derived Cu-based materials have been obtained via high-temperature thermal reduction or room-temperature
electroreduction, which are hard to maintain the co-existence of Cu(0) and Cu(I) on the
surface. As a consequence, significant variances exist for their reported electrocatalytic
performances to date [16,29,30,36,37].
Herein, we demonstrate a reverse strategy of room-temperature growth of an oxide
layer on the surface of freshly-prepared Cu nanorods, yielding a high interface of Cu(I) and
Cu(0) on the catalyst surface (Fig. 1a). This co-existence of both Cu(I) and Cu(0) in vicinity
enables a synergistic effect between these two surface reactive centers, which favors the
formation of a positive carbon atom and a negative carbon, respectively, and the subsequent
dimerization of C−C bond for different C2 products (Fig. 1b).

sections.heading: 2. Experimental section
sections.text:
2.1. Chemicals and materials All chemicals used in this work were of analytical reagent grade (AR), commercially
available and without further purification. Cupric nitrate trihydrate (99.0−102.0%), sodium
hydroxide (> 96%), potassium hydrogen carbonate (> 99.5%), and the ammonia water
solution (25−28%) were purchased from the Sinopharm Chemical Reagent Company. The
Nafion solution (Dupont, D-521 dispersion, 5% w/w in water and 1-propanol), 211 Nafion membrane (Dupont) were purchased from Alfa Aesar. CO2 gas (99.99%), Ar gas (99.99%),
N2 gas (99.99%), and 5 vol.% H2/Ar gas were purchased from Shanghai Tomoe Gas Company.
2.2. Synthesis of Cu(OH)2 In a typical synthesis, 3.02 g of Cu(NO3)2·3H2O were dissolved in 250 mL of deionized
(DI) water. Then 5 mL of 25% ammonia solution was slowly added into above solution under
vigorous stirring, followed by the addition of 5 mL of NaOH (0.01 M) solution. The mixed solution was heated at 60 oC for 1 h. The resulting bluish precipitate was collected by centrifugation, washed to neutral pH with water, and finally dried under vacuum at 60 oC for
12 h.
2.3. Synthesis of Cu, Cu@Cu2O and CuOx samples The obtained Cu(OH)2 precursor was first placed into a quartz tube in a horizontal
furnace. The furnace was heated to 250 ºC at a rate of 5 ºC min−1, and maintained for 1 h in 5
vol.% H2/Ar atmosphere at a flow rate of 100 standard-state cubic centimeter per minute (sccm) to get Cu sample. The freshly synthesized Cu sample was stored in hexane to avoid
oxidation. To get the Cu@Cu2O sample, the synthesized Cu was partially oxidized by exposing to air at room temperature under ambient atmosphere for 3 weeks. For comparison, Cu sample was heated at 200 ºC in air with a heating rate of 5 ºC min−1 for 1 h to get the
CuOx sample.
2.4. Electrochemical measurements
All electrochemical measurements were carried out in an H-cell system at an
electrochemical station (CH Instrument, Inc.). A Pt plate and an Ag/AgCl (in 3 M KCl
solution) electrode were used as the counter electrode and reference electrode, respectively.
The electroreduction of CO2 was conducted in CO2-saturated 0.1 M KHCO3 aqueous solution (pH 6.8). Before the test, CO2 was purged into the electrolyte for 30 mins to remove residual air in the electrolyte. All potentials in this study were measured against the Ag/AgCl electrode and converted to the reversible hydrogen electrode (RHE) reference scale by adding
a value of (0.21 + 0.059 × pH) V. The gas products were monitored by Shanghai Ramiin GC 2060 gas chromatograph. The liquid products were quantified by 1H nuclear magnetic
resonance (NMR) spectroscopy (Bruker AVANCEAV III HD 500), in which 0.6 mL of electrolyte was mixed with 0.06 mL of D2O and 10 -6 M dimethyl sulfoxide (Sigma, 99.99%) as an internal standard.
2.5. Estimation of electrochemical surface areas (ECSAs)
Cyclic voltammetry (CV) was used to study the roughness of the materials, which was
conducted in the electrolysis cell with CO2-saturated 0.1 M KHCO3 at various scan rates. A potential window from −0.2 to −0.3 V (vs. Ag/AgCl) was applied, as no faradaic processes
were occurring in this range. The geometric current density was plotted against the scan rate
of the CV. The double- layer capacitance is directly proportional to the roughness of the
material.

sections.heading: 3. Results and Discussion
sections.text:
Cu nanorods were prepared by liquid precipitation-thermal reduction (Experimental
section), which presented a light red color (Fig. S1). Scanning electron microscopy (SEM) and transmission electron microscopy (TEM) images showed that the as-made Cu nanorods
had a coral- like microstructure, with a uniform diameter distribution of ~ 100 nm (Fig. 2a, b).
High-resolution TEM (HRTEM) images displayed the lattice spacing of 0.181 nm (Fig. 2c),
consistent with the (200) plane of the face-centered cubic phase of Cu [30]. After the room-
temperature oxidation (Experimental section), the surface morphology of the oxidized Cu (designated as Cu@Cu2O) was retained, while a surface layer of 10 ± 5 nm thickness was observed on each nanorod (Fig. 2d, e), suggesting the surface oxidation of Cu. HRTEM
image of Cu@Cu2O (Fig. 2f) exhibited the lattice fringes of the core as 0.208 nm, consistent with the (111) plane of the face-centered cubic phase of Cu. The crystalline shell presented a
characteristic spacing of 0.245 nm, consistent with the (111) plane of Cu2O [30]. The energy dispersive X-ray spectroscopy (EDS) mapping showed the elemental distributions of Cu and
O (Fig. 2g), confirming the growth of thin oxide layer on the surface of nanorods. For
comparison, the same Cu nanorods were also fully oxidized to oxides via thermal annealing
in air at 200 ºC for 1 h (Fig. S2). Although the copper oxide nanorods (designated as CuOx) still presented a similar morphology, no core-shell structures were observed. HRTEM image of the CuOx sample exhibited the lattice fringes as 0.216 and 0.245 nm (inset in Fig. S2c), consistent with the (200) and (111) plane of Cu2O, respectively [30].
The crystal structures of all samples were confirmed by X-ray diffraction (XRD, Fig.
3a). For the samples of Cu and Cu@Cu2O, the sharp and intense diffraction peaks at 43.3°, 50.5°, 74.1°, 89.9° and 95.1° were indexed to the (111), (200), (220), (311) and (222) planes of Cu (JCPDS card No. 04-0836), respectively. No diffraction peaks of Cu2O were identified, implying the poor crystalline and low content of Cu2O in Cu@Cu2O. For the CuOx sample, diffraction peaks at 29.7°, 36.4°, 42.3°, 61.4°and 73.5° were clearly observed and indexed to
(110), (111), (200), (220) and (311) planes of Cu2O (JCPDS card No. 05-0667), respectively, while no remaining Cu species were identified [38].
X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS) measurements were further conducted to
investigate the composition and oxidation states of copper on the surface (Fig. 3b). The peaks
at 952.0 and 932.2 eV of the Cu sample (black curve) were assigned to the binding energies
of Cu(0) 2p1/2 and 2p3/2, respectively [39,40]. For the Cu@Cu2O composite (red curve), the XPS spectra indicated the co-existence of both Cu(I) (binding energies 952.3 and 932.5 eV) and Cu(II) (binding energies 954.3 and 933.7 eV) on the surface, consistent with previous
studies that the native copper oxide is generally composed of a duplex type structure with
Cu2O and CuO [39,41,42]. The percentages of Cu(I) and Cu(II) in Cu@Cu2O were estimated as 88% and 12%, respectively. For the thermally oxidized CuOx (blue curve), both Cu(I) and Cu(II) also co-existed, the broad shakeup satellite peaks at ~962 eV and ~943 eV in Cu 2p further indicated the much higher presence of Cu(II) species, and the percentages of Cu(II)
was estimated as 82%, indicating the much deeper oxidation level in high temperature (~ 200 oC) than that in room temperature (i.e., Cu@Cu2O). The reason that no signal of Cu2O was found in XRD or XPS may be due to the little amount of Cu2O as well as the poor crystallinity. Thus, Auger electron spectroscopy (AES) was also applied for the analysis of the as-prepared catalyst (Fig. S3). The peak centered at ~916.9 eV was attributed to the Cu2O, in good accord with the reference [43].
More detailed structural information was further obtained from the X-ray absorption
near-edge structure (XANES, Fig. 3c). The spectra of Cu@Cu2O and CuOx samples resembled those of Cu reference and Cu2O reference, respectively, which were attributed to the small quantity of Cu2O in the Cu@Cu2O sample. Interestingly, compared to the peak of Cu reference, the peak intensity at ~ 8984.5 eV of Cu@Cu2O declined (Fig. 3c), which was attributed to slightly oxidation of metallic Cu after room-temperature oxidation [41,44]. As
for the CuOx sample, the peak intensity at ~ 8985.2 eV of CuOx decreased comparing to that of Cu2O reference, which may be caused by the presence of trace surface CuO. On the other hand, as shown in Fig. 3d, the peaks related to the Cu–Cu coordination in the metal (at ca.
2.2 Å) of Cu@Cu2O were observed, suggesting that Cu@Cu2O consists of major Cu phase.
As for the CuOx sample, the peak related to Cu–O (at ~ 1.5 Å) in cuprous oxide are obtained, indicating that CuOx was composed of major Cu2O phase. Comparing to the Cu–Cu peak of Cu2O reference (at ca. 2.7 Å), the location of Cu–Cu peak of CuOx (at ~ 2.67 Å) slightly changed, further confirming that there existed trace CuO [41,44,45].
The electrochemical CO2RR was then conducted in CO2-saturated 0.1 M KHCO3
aqueous solution (pH 6.8) at a constant potential with a two-compartment H-type cell
(Experimental section). All the voltages reported in this work were referred to reversible
hydrogen electrode (RHE). The linear sweep voltammetry (LSV) curves of the Cu, Cu@Cu2O and CuOx were first measured (Fig. 4a), among which the Cu@Cu2O sample exhibited the highest current density. For instance, at −1.0 V, the current densities of the Cu, Cu@Cu2O and CuOx electrocatalysts were measured as 11, 18 and 7 mA cm -2. The distribution of the CO2RR products were quantified by in- line gas chromatography and 1H nuclear magnetic resonance (Experimental section), and summarized in Fig. 4b-e. For the Cu@Cu2O catalyst, the detailed characterization data, including the 1H-NMR (Fig. S4) and gas chromatography (Fig. S5), are available in the SI. It can be seen that the hydrogen
evolution reaction (HER) was greatly suppressed, with the faradaic efficiency (FE) for H2 measured about 30% at all applied potentials between −0.6 and −1.6 V. The C2 products, including ethylene (C2H4) and ethanol (C2H5OH), started to be detected from −0.8 V. The maximum total C2 products were collected at −1.0 V, with FEC2H4 and FEC2H5OH as 21% and 29%, respectively. In contrast, for the Cu catalyst, H2 was the dominant product (FEH2 = 53 – 62%, Fig. 4c), while the total FE value of C2 products (mainly C2H5OH) was less than 20%. For the CuOx catalyst, the major C2 product was C2H4, of which a peak FEC2H4 of 26% at −1.6 V. In addition, the electrochemical stability test was conducted under −1.4 V (vs. RHE) for over 6 h, where the core-shell Cu@Cu2O maintained a good catalytic performance (Fig. S6).
To illustrate the significant improved C2 product selectivity of the Cu@Cu2O, the
electrochemically active surface areas (ECSAs) of these samples were calculated by
measuring the electrochemical double-layer capacitance (Cdl, Experimental section) [16]. The Cdl of Cu, Cu@Cu2O and CuOx were calculated as 0.058, 0.061, 0.011 mF/cm 2, respectively (Fig. S7), which were similar and may not well explain their different electrocatalytic
performances. Another possible reason was originated from the different oxidation states of
these catalysts. First, recent reports about the oxidation state of copper under CO2 reduction condition clearly demonstrated that Cu(I) species can remain relatively stable at negative potentials [28,31,34]. In this work, we found that the Cu2O species in Cu@Cu2O catalyst was still observed even after electrolysis at −1.2 V (vs RHE) for 2 h (Fig. S8), demonstrating its
good electrochemical stability during the CO2RR process. Second, the detection of gas products over the Cu@Cu2O catalyst indicates that selectivity toward C2H4 was observed to be stable at −1.2 V over 7 h (Fig. 4f), providing the indirect proof of long-term stability of the active sites for C2 production during CO2RR. Third, according to H. Xiao and coworkers’ calculation [35], due to the d−π electronic effect, the C atom of *CO@Cu+ is positively charged whereas the C atom of *CO@Cu0 is negatively charged. Thus, the electrostatic
attraction between the two carbon atoms of *CO assists the *CO dimerization and the C−C
bond formation, thus improving the reaction kinetics toward the C2 production. Therefore, we propose that the synergetic effect between surface Cu(I) and Cu(0) is responsible for high
activity and selectivity of Cu@Cu2O.
To further prove the synergism between surface Cu+ and Cu0 in Cu@Cu2O, the
Cu@Cu2O catalyst was reduced to Cu in a 5 vol.% H2/Ar atmosphere (denoted as ReducedCu, Fig. S9), and its CO2RR catalytic performance was tested under same condition. The selectivity for C2 products by the Reduced-Cu sample decreased drastically to nearly zero, while the FE of H2 increased up to be 59% at −0.6 V (Fig. 4e). All these experimental results
confirmed that the synergism between surface Cu+ and Cu0 in Cu@Cu2O, which contributed to the high activity and selectivity toward C2 products during the electrocatalytic CO2RR.

sections.heading: 4. Conclusions
sections.text:
In summary, we have designed a core-shell Cu@Cu2O nanorod catalyst with effective
Cu/Cu+ interface by a room-temperature grown native oxide layer on Cu surface. Compared to recent work on the copper/cuprous oxide catalysts [46-48], this Cu@Cu2O catalyst exhibited an excellent selectivity for C2 to be ~ 50% at −1.0 V vs RHE with a capability of inhibiting HER. In addition, a synergism between surface Cu(I) and Cu(0) in Cu@Cu2O was identified, which contributed to improving the efficiency and selectivity toward C2 products. Further design and fabrication of high interface between these two reactive centers may lead to higher electrochemical CO2RR performances with even better optimized C2+ selectivity. This work can provide a new perspective on the electrochemical CO2 reduction, and suggest new strategies to construct a relatively high selective and reactive interface for the CO2 reduction reaction, especially toward C2 products.
